title: The Sinatra session where Jones played "I Like the Sunrise"
summary: At the 1967 Sinatra-Ellington session Jones, called by Jimmy Hamilton, walked in and played the one Ellington number.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: So you just walked in and recorded with Duke's band for -- that was in late '58.
Yeah. On, "Jazz Party."
The next time you did it I was there, and that was in late '67, and that was --
That was with Ella?
No, that was with -- the next time I remember your doing it, that was when he was recording with Frank Sinatra and --
Oh, yeah. Yeah. I'd forgotten all about that.

And it was here in town and it was Sinatra's birthday and they had been trying to make an album together for years and could never make their schedules coincide, and so when they finally decided to do it there wasn't time -- the only way they could meet was so soon that there wasn't time for Duke to do some arrangements for Frank or to have any done for Frank, and so Frank said, 'Okay, I'll have Billy May do some things.'
Yeah. Yeah.
So it turned out to be not Ellington music, and the only Ellington number on it -- Frank wouldn't do it without one Ellington number -- the only Ellington number on there was, 'I Like the Sunrise.'
Yes. Yes.

And so we were all assembled for the great recording session, and just as we were about -- they hadn't run through it or anything, and the next number to be recorded was, 'I Like the Sunrise,' and the door opened and Jimmy Jones walked in. And Duke says, 'Aha, Jimmy Jones. Come over here, Jimmy Jones.' And you didn't know what was happening in there.
No, I didn't.

I mean you didn't know what was coming up or anything, and you came over and Duke got up and gestured the piano seat to you, and you did, 'I Like the Sunrise,' so the only Ellington number on, 'Edward K. and Francis A.' album, or, 'Francis A. and Edward K.,' the only Ellington piece is played by Jimmy Jones. Duke Ellington plays the non-Ellington pieces.
Yeah. You know, I said a thing to Duke -- when I did, 'I Like the Sunrise,' it was with Ella and Duke.
Yeah, right. Right.
You know? And I told Duke, I said, 'Don't

we have a score on this?" (Laughter) You know. Because after I left I gave him the parts, you know. And he says, "Yeah, we've got a good score on it." It's just like somebody else had written it, you know. We didn't talk about who had done it, you know. And --
But you didn't come to the Sinatra session expecting to play.
No, I just came there.
Because I remember the amazed expression you had.

Yeah. Because -- well, Jimmy Hamilton called me. He says, "Man, do you know what we're doing? We're in town, over here recording." And I had to come from way over on Carmona, you know, to where the studio was.
Uh-huh.

And the next thing I knew I was -- I was playing. And Sinatra -- like you said, it was Sinatra's birthday, and he brought some booze or something, and he put it right within Paul Gonzalves Gonzalez's reach. I said, "That's the wrong place to put it." So after the date was over we started -- Sam and Jeff Castleman -- that's his name, I think.
Yeah, right. Bass player.
We started jamming. And playing, "Happy Birthday," and everything else, you know.
Yeah, well, we had a party in the studio.
Yeah.

Duke had sent four bottles of Dom Perignon champagne to Frank with roses. I know because I ordered it, for the birthday celebration. And Frank magnanimously passed the Dom Perignon to the band, and Duke was mad. He said, 'I didn't buy that Dom Perignon for this band.'
(Laughter)
Well, they were -- the band got through it all right, you know.
Uh-huh. It's just a shame it wasn't Duke's music, though, I think, but it was a matter of time. I mean, you know, there was one piece of Duke's music.
Yeah, they just couldn't get together on schedules, like you were saying. And you know, that's kind of hard, when guys are travelling all the time, you know.
Yeah.
But the date came off all right.
Oh, yeah.
It came off okay. 'I Like the Sunrise.'
